scope: Public managed retirement of native-created interrupted records after guardian-loss recovery and return
qualification: Managed saved-job retirement now recognizes interrupted as terminal on the current boot, matching native. The request deletes only the saved record; it does not signal a process or invent an exit code.

Differential tests cover nine saved record scenarios, no start replay, refusal of current-boot starting/running/cancelling/unknown records, and refusal to forget a worker-owned live job. The real guardian-loss integration case now also forgets the returned interrupted record through managed while preserving the other retained records.

Both TVs migrated, lost a freshly bound committed guardian to one SIGKILL, automatically reacquired native through the unchanged coordinator and returned normally to managed. Interrupted records retained null exit codes and a single execution witness. The enrolled public managed job.forget request then succeeded; file absence and unchanged pre-existing retained jobs were verified.

All owned test/deployment units are inactive. Both TVs remain managed-ready and settled on their original boot with SDK on loopback, entry/archive DLLs unchanged and independent 300-second .NET SDK rescue available.

The changed managed DLL triggered the existing managed-package-version-mismatch guard. On each TV, a separate authenticated worker from the exact signed package passed runtime, mount, unit and retained-state verification. The original selection and complete history were archived; a held managed-to-managed transaction committed only after independent SDK proof of probe exit and cleanup. Normal service acquisition was then independently verified. No historical digest was overwritten and the mismatch guard remains unchanged.
limits: Both package-upgrade baselines contained zero saved jobs. Nonempty retained upgrade records and inconsistent readback are locally tested; the subsequent hardware guardian rounds exercise nonempty retained state across native recovery and managed return.

Managed upgrade verification and selection-plan primitives are host-side maintenance tools. Publication and interrupted-publication recovery remain explicit orchestration; there is no automatic public upgrade endpoint.

Forgetting a terminal record is metadata retirement, not a new proof of descendant cleanup. The native reconciliation and normal return checks supply that proof in these hardware trials. Same-boot uncertain records and worker-owned live jobs remain refused.

Native-only capability entry, partial-journal service recovery, broader pressure/performance/endurance and native-default rollout remain open. The managed fallback remains deployed. No reboot, standby, global policy or persistent capability change occurred.
